etymology: From Middle English bewreyen, to accuse or disclose — the prefix be- joined to Old English wrēgan, to accuse or make known; not the same word as “betray,” though it drifts near it, meaning to reveal, expose, or give away.
biblical_def: To bewray is to disclose what was meant to be hidden — to let a thing out, whether by tongue, by trembling, or by the tell-tale accent of a man’s speech. The word can carry guilt or innocence in the same breath. The partner of a thief “heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not” (Pro 29:24): his silence bewrays his heart, for the man who will not testify to a crime has joined it. In Isaiah the prophet pleads the opposite duty — “hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3) — where to bewray is to betray the fugitive to his hunters. But the word’s most piercing use is in the high priest’s courtyard, where a servant girl says to Peter, “Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee” (Mat 26:73). His Galilean tongue disclosed what his oaths denied; the man could change his words but not his voice, and the voice preached the truth against him. Herein is the law of the mouth: what a man is will out, for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh” (Mat 12:34). Sin is a poor secret-keeper. Grace, too, bewrays itself — the accent of heaven clings to the born-again man, and his speech, seasoned with salt, discloses whose he is before he means to confess it.
webster_summary: To reveal or expose what was hidden — famously, Peter’s Galilean speech bewraying him in the high priest’s hall.
webster_full: BEWRAY, to disclose, reveal, or expose; to make known what was concealed.
Distinct from “betray,” though it approaches it: to give a thing away.
“Thy speech bewrayeth thee” — Peter’s accent discloses him (Mat 26:73).
To bewray the wanderer (Isa 16:3) is to hand him to his pursuers.
What the heart hides, the mouth bewrays: the law of Matthew 12:34.
scriptures: Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not.
Isa 16:3
Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth.
And after a while came unto him they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them; for thy speech bewrayeth thee.
O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a lost verb; recovering it recovers the truth that what a man is will out, in his speech and his silence alike.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the word rebukes is the modern conceit that a man can curate himself — that the self is what we broadcast, not what leaks out under pressure. Scripture knows better. The heart bewrays itself in an unguarded accent, a nervous silence, a word spoken in anger; the mask slips in the courtyard when the fire burns low. An age that has made image-management a craft has only multiplied the servant-girls who see through it. “Be sure your sin will find you out” (Num 32:23).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honesty of the mouth: that speech is diagnostic, not decorative. Peter’s tongue bewrayed his fear; may ours bewray a better master. The man renewed by grace cannot wholly hide it either — the accent of the new birth clings to him, and his speech, seasoned with salt, discloses whose he is (Col 4:6).
roots_summary: From Old English wrēgan, to accuse, comes a verb meaning to reveal or expose — near “betray” but not the same word.
roots_lines: Bewray — Middle English bewreyen; Old English wrēgan, to accuse.
It means to disclose or expose, not primarily to betray a trust.
Silence can bewray a man’s guilt as loudly as words (Pro 29:24).
Peter’s Galilean speech bewrayed him in the high priest’s hall (Mat 26:73).
What the heart hides, the mouth bewrays — the law of Matthew 12:34.
usage: His silence bewrayed him as surely as a confession would have.
The heart’s abundance bewrays itself in the unguarded word.
Grace, too, bewrays itself: the accent of heaven clings to the man.

etymology: From Old English cīdan, to contend, quarrel, or scold; a strong verb of speech meaning to dispute loudly, to reprove with heat, or to strive in words.
biblical_def: To chide is to contend in words — to quarrel, upbraid, or wrangle, often with heat and complaint. The wilderness is its schoolroom. At Rephidim “the people did chide with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink,” and Moses answered, “Why chide ye with me? wherefore do ye tempt the LORD?” (Exo 17:2). To chide with the LORD’s servant, Moses saw, was to tempt the LORD Himself; murmuring dressed as a demand is unbelief with a raised voice. The men of Ephraim “did chide with him sharply” against Gideon (Jdg 8:1), wounded pride sharpening the tongue. So the word gathers up the whole ugly music of the flesh — grievance, envy, self-justification — poured out against the man God set over them. Set against all this is the astonishing patience of God: “He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever” (Psa 103:9). Man chides from weakness and wounded self-love; God chides in righteousness and then, toward His own, lays the quarrel down. He rebukes that He may restore, and His anger endureth but a moment (Psa 30:5). Let the reader mark the difference and learn to chide as God chides, if he must chide at all — slowly, justly, and with an end always in mercy.
webster_summary: To contend or quarrel in words, to scold or upbraid — yet of God it is said, “He will not always chide.”
webster_full: CHIDE, to contend in words; to quarrel, wrangle, or scold with heat.
To reprove sharply, or to upbraid one with grievance and complaint.
Israel chid with Moses for water in the wilderness (Exo 17:2).
To chide with God’s servant is to tempt the LORD Himself.
Of God: “He will not always chide, neither keep his anger for ever” (Psa 103:9).
scriptures: Exo 17:2
Wherefore the people did chide with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink. And Moses said unto them, Why chide ye with me? wherefore do ye tempt the LORD?
Jdg 8:1
And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply.
He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever.
And Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban: and Jacob answered and said to Laban, What is my trespass? what is my sin, that thou hast so hotly pursued after me?
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under siege but a plain old verb for quarreling; it recovers the difference between man’s peevish chiding and God’s righteous, self-limiting rebuke.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the age’s appetite for the quarrel itself — the endless contending, the grievance nursed and broadcast, the tongue that must have the last word. Israel chid with Moses because the heart chid with God; the complaint against the man was unbelief against the LORD. So it is still: much of what parades as principled protest is the wilderness murmur in newer clothes, the flesh demanding water and calling it justice. To chide freely is easy; to hold the tongue in trust is the harder and rarer grace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pattern of God’s chiding: He will not always chide, nor keep His anger for ever. Where man’s reproof runs to bitterness and never lets go, God rebukes in measure and toward an end of mercy. Fathers are charged to imitate it — “provoke not your children to wrath” (Eph 6:4) — and every saint is called to a speech slow to strife and quick to peace.
roots_summary: From Old English cīdan, to contend, comes a verb for quarreling in words — the wilderness sin against Moses and the LORD.
roots_lines: Chide — Old English cīdan, to contend or quarrel.
Its past tense is “chode” (Gen 31:36; Num 20:3).
Israel chid with Moses for water and so tempted the LORD (Exo 17:2).
Ephraim chid sharply with Gideon out of wounded pride (Jdg 8:1).
God will not always chide, nor keep his anger for ever (Psa 103:9).
usage: To chide with God’s servant is often to quarrel with God.
Man chides from weakness; God chides in righteousness and then lets it go.
He rebukes that He may restore, for His anger endureth but a moment.

etymology: The old strong past tense of chide (Old English cīdan), formed like “ride/rode” — meaning “contended” or “quarreled,” now wholly displaced by the regular “chided.”
biblical_def: Chode is simply the past of chide — “contended, quarreled” — and it stands in the KJV at two hot moments of strife. When Laban overtook the fleeing Jacob, “Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban” (Gen 31:36), the patriarch at last pouring out twenty years of swallowed grievance: “What is my trespass? what is my sin, that thou hast so hotly pursued after me?” Here the chiding is a man’s honest protest against injustice, and God does not condemn it. The second is graver: at Kadesh, want of water, “the people chode with Moses” and wished themselves dead with their brethren (Num 20:3). This was the murmur that undid Moses himself, for in answering it he smote the rock in anger and was shut out of the land — “the children of Israel strove with the LORD, and he was sanctified in them” (Num 20:13). The waters were named Meribah, Strife. The old form quietly preserves a warning the modern “chided” softens: strife against God’s appointed leader is strife against God, and it defiles even the meekest man on earth (Num 12:3) if he lets it kindle his own spirit. They angered Him at the waters of strife, “so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes” (Psa 106:32). The people chode; the servant fell; the land was lost.
webster_summary: The archaic past tense of chide — “contended, quarreled” — standing at Jacob’s protest and Israel’s fatal strife at Meribah.
webster_full: CHODE, the old strong preterite of chide: contended, quarreled, wrangled.
Formed as “ride” makes “rode”; now displaced by regular “chided.”
Jacob chode with Laban, protesting twenty years of wrong (Gen 31:36).
The people chode with Moses at Kadesh for want of water (Num 20:3).
That strife was named Meribah, and it cost Moses the land (Num 20:13).
scriptures: And Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban: and Jacob answered and said to Laban, What is my trespass? what is my sin, that thou hast so hotly pursued after me?
Num 20:3
And the people chode with Moses, and spake, saying, Would God that we had died when our brethren died before the LORD!
This is the water of Meribah; because the children of Israel strove with the LORD, and he was sanctified in them.
Exo 17:7
And he called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because of the chiding of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the LORD, saying, Is the LORD among us, or not?
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine but a vanished verb-form; recovering “chode” recovers the sharp KJV lesson of Meribah, where the people’s strife undid the servant of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the light view of strife. Israel chode with Moses as if grumbling were a small thing, a natural release of thirst and fear; but the LORD counted it strife against Himself and it cost His servant the promised land. The age that treats complaint as a right and the murmur as harmless has forgotten Meribah. There is a strife that dries the soul as surely as thirst dried Israel, and the man who lets others’ chiding kindle his own may find, like Moses, that one hot word forfeits much.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness of Meribah: that strife against God’s ordering is strife against God, and it defiles even the meek. The old form “chode” keeps the wound fresh where the smooth “chided” might let us pass it by. Let the reader draw water instead from the Rock that followed them, which was Christ (1Co 10:4), and cease from strife.
roots_summary: The old preterite of chide, “chode” carries the KJV’s two great scenes of strife — Jacob with Laban and Israel at Meribah.
roots_lines: Chode — strong past tense of chide; Old English cīdan.
Now wholly replaced by the regular form “chided.”
Jacob chode with Laban after twenty years of wrong (Gen 31:36).
The people chode with Moses at the waters of Meribah (Num 20:3).
That strife cost Moses the land — it went ill with him (Psa 106:32).
usage: The people chode; the servant fell; the land was lost.
Strife against God’s appointed leader is strife against God Himself.
One hot word at Meribah forfeited what forty years had earned.

etymology: The archaic past tense of dare, from Old English dorste, preterite of durran, to have courage or boldness; meaning “dared” — had the daring or presumption to do a thing.
biblical_def: Durst means “dared” — had the boldness or hardihood for an act — and it appears most often in the KJV as a boundary no man would cross. When the Lord had silenced the Pharisees and Sadducees, “no man was able to answer him a word, neither durst any man from that day forth ask him any more questions” (Mat 22:46): His wisdom raised a fence about Him that daring could not pass. By the sea of Tiberias, before the risen Christ, “none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord” (Joh 21:12) — holy awe stilling even affectionate curiosity. In Jerusalem, when signs and wonders were done by the apostles’ hands, “of the rest durst no man join himself to them” (Act 5:13): the fear of God on the church held the double-minded at a reverent distance. The word’s most instructive use guards the tongue of an angel: “Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee” (Jud 1:9). If the chief of angels durst not rail even at the devil, how brazen the men who speak evil of dignities they do not understand. Durst marks the edge of holy reverence — the point where daring must yield to fear of the LORD, and the bold man learns there is a line he will not, dare not, pass.
webster_summary: The old past tense of “dare” — had the boldness; often marking the line reverence forbids one to cross.
webster_full: DURST, the archaic preterite of dare: dared; had the courage or presumption.
From Old English dorste, past tense of durran, to have boldness.
None durst ask Christ more questions after His wisdom silenced them (Mat 22:46).
None durst join the awed apostolic church lightly (Act 5:13).
Michael durst not rail even at the devil (Jud 1:9).
scriptures: And no man was able to answer him a word, neither durst any man from that day forth ask him any more questions.
Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord.
Act 5:13
And of the rest durst no man join himself to them: but the people magnified them.
Jud 1:9
Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a fading verb; it recovers the vanished sense of reverent fear — the line a wise soul dares not cross.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the brazenness of the age, which durst do anything and reverences nothing. Jude sets the archangel’s restraint against “filthy dreamers” who “speak evil of the things that they know not” (Jud 1:8, 10); if Michael durst not bring a railing accusation against Satan himself, the flippant tongue that mocks God, mocks His ministers, and jeers at every dignity has lost the very organ of the fear of God. What men now call boldness is often only the death of reverence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is holy dread — that there are questions the awed heart durst not ask and words it durst not speak, not from cowardice but from the fear of the LORD. “None durst” is the mark of a people who know Whose presence they are in. The recovery of that word would restore the recovery of that fear, which is the beginning of wisdom (Pro 9:10).
roots_summary: The archaic past tense of dare, “durst” marks in the KJV the boundary that reverence and the fear of God forbid.
roots_lines: Durst — Old English dorste, preterite of durran, to dare.
It means “dared” — had the boldness or hardihood.
None durst question Christ after His wisdom silenced them (Mat 22:46).
The awe of God held men from lightly joining the church (Act 5:13).
Michael durst not rail even at the devil, but said, The Lord rebuke thee (Jud 1:9).
usage: None durst ask Him, for they knew that it was the Lord.
If the archangel durst not rail at Satan, how brazen the mocking tongue.
Durst marks the edge where daring must yield to the fear of God.

etymology: From Old English trūwian, to trust, believe, or think — kin to “true” and “troth”; meaning to suppose, believe, or reckon a thing so.
biblical_def: Trow means “think, suppose, believe it likely,” and it appears just once in the KJV, closing the Lord’s parable of the unprofitable servant with a quiet, cutting question. Having pictured a master whose servant comes in from plowing only to gird himself and serve at table, Jesus asks, “Doth he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him? I trow not” (Luk 17:9). “I trow not” — I suppose not, I do not think so. The single word carries the whole weight of the lesson. The servant who has plowed all day and served all evening is owed no thanks and may claim no merit, for he has only done his duty (Luk 17:7-8). So the Lord draws the application: “when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10). Here is the death of merit and the ground of grace. Even perfect obedience — had we such — would earn no wage from God, for obedience is not a gift we bring but a debt we owe. The Roman notion of works of supererogation, treasuries of surplus merit, falls before “I trow not.” What thanks, then, that the Master should rise and gird Himself and serve us (Luk 12:37)? That reversal is not our wage but His grace — the whole gospel hid in a servant’s two archaic words.
webster_summary: To think, suppose, or believe likely — the KJV hapax “I trow not” sealing the parable of the unprofitable servant.
webster_full: TROW, to think, believe, or suppose; to reckon a thing probable.
From Old English trūwian, to trust; kin to “true” and “troth.”
It stands once in the KJV: “I trow not” (Luk 17:9).
The servant who does his duty earns no thanks and may claim no merit.
So falls every notion of works that would put God in our debt.
scriptures: Luk 17:9
Doth he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him? I trow not.
Luk 17:7
But which of you, having a servant plowing or feeding cattle, will say unto him by and by, when he is come from the field, Go and sit down to meat?
Luk 17:8
And will not rather say unto him, Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me, till I have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink?
So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a lost word; “I trow not” guards the great truth that duty done earns no merit — the death of works-righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the perennial pride of merit — the servant’s wish to be thanked, the sinner’s claim on God. “I trow not” strips it bare: even a full day’s obedience puts no thanks in the servant’s hand, for he has done only what was owed. Rome built treasuries of surplus merit on the denial of this word; the modern heart builds them still, keeping private ledgers of good deeds it means to present. All such accounting dies at Luke 17:9.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the confession of the unprofitable servant, which is the doorway to grace. When we have done all, we have added nothing to God and earned nothing from Him; and it is precisely there, where merit ends, that the Master’s astonishing grace begins — for He girds Himself and serves His servants (Luk 12:37). Salvation is of grace, not of works, lest any man should boast (Eph 2:9).
roots_summary: From Old English trūwian, to trust, “trow” means to suppose — the KJV hapax that seals the death of merit.
roots_lines: Trow — Old English trūwian, to trust or believe; kin to “true.”
It means to think, suppose, or reckon a thing likely.
It occurs once in the KJV: “I trow not” (Luk 17:9).
The dutiful servant earns no thanks and claims no merit (Luk 17:7-8).
We are unprofitable servants, having done but our duty (Luk 17:10).
usage: Doth God owe the servant thanks for his duty? I trow not.
When we have done all, we are unprofitable servants still.
Where merit ends, the Master’s astonishing grace begins.

etymology: From Old English witan, to know (present tense wāt) — kin to “wit” and German wissen; meaning “to know,” a knowing by acquaintance or awareness rather than mere information.
biblical_def: Wot means “know” — the old present tense of the verb that gave us “wit” — and the KJV uses it across the whole range of human knowing and not-knowing. Abimelech pleads ignorance of the seized well: “I wot not who hath done this thing” (Gen 21:26). At Sinai the people, tired of waiting, say of Moses, “we wot not what is become of him” (Exo 32:1) — and that not-knowing curdles quickly into a golden calf, for the heart that will not wait on the unseen God soon makes a god it can see. Peter, preaching, grants his hearers a measure of grace: “I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers” (Act 3:17); their crime was real, yet their ignorance leaves a door open to repentance. And Paul presses the Romans with the word turned into a rebuke: “Wot ye not what the scripture saith of Elias?” (Rom 11:2). There the sting is that they ought to have known — the Scripture stood plain, and ignorance of it was culpable. So the little word divides two ignorances: the honest not-knowing that mercy pities, and the lazy not-knowing of the man who will not search the Scripture he professes to own. “Wot ye not” is God’s reproach to every believer content to be a stranger to His book.
webster_summary: The old present tense of the verb “to know” — ranging from honest ignorance pitied to willful not-knowing rebuked.
webster_full: WOT, to know; the archaic present tense from Old English witan, to know.
Kin to “wit,” “wisdom,” and German wissen; a knowing by awareness.
“We wot not what is become of him” — Israel before the calf (Exo 32:1).
“I wot that through ignorance ye did it” — ignorance pitied (Act 3:17).
“Wot ye not what the scripture saith” — ignorance rebuked (Rom 11:2).
scriptures: And Abimelech said, I wot not who hath done this thing: neither didst thou tell me, neither yet heard I of it, but to day.
Exo 32:1

And when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron, and said unto him, Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him.
Act 3:17
And now, brethren, I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers.
Rom 11:2
God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew. Wot ye not what the scripture saith of Elias? how he maketh intercession to God against Israel, saying,
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under attack but a vanished word for knowing; it recovers the difference between innocent ignorance and the culpable not-knowing of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the ignorance men choose. Israel “wot not” what became of Moses and made a calf; the not-knowing was really an unwillingness to wait on God. Much modern ignorance of Scripture is of the same kind — not that men cannot know, but that they will not open the book. “Wot ye not what the scripture saith” falls heavily on an age that owns more Bibles than any before it and reads them least. To be a stranger to the word one professes is a chosen darkness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that some ignorance is guilt. Scripture pities the honest not-knowing of Abimelech and even, in a measure, of those who crucified the Lord (Act 3:17; Luk 23:34); but it reproves the believer who will not know what the Scripture plainly saith. The remedy is to search the Scriptures daily (Act 17:11), that we may say with knowledge, not excuse ourselves with ignorance.
roots_summary: From Old English witan, to know, “wot” is the old present tense — dividing honest ignorance from willful not-knowing.
roots_lines: Wot — Old English witan, to know; present tense wāt.
Kin to “wit,” “wisdom,” and German wissen.
Israel wot not what became of Moses and made a calf (Exo 32:1).
Peter grants that ignorance did the deed, leaving room to repent (Act 3:17).
“Wot ye not what the scripture saith” rebukes chosen ignorance (Rom 11:2).
usage: The heart that wots not the unseen God soon makes one it can see.
Some not-knowing mercy pities; some the Scripture rebukes.
“Wot ye not” is God’s reproach to the stranger to His book.

etymology: A compound of “how,” “be,” and “it” — literally “how (ever) it be” — an Old-English-rooted conjunction meaning “nevertheless,” “however,” or “yet notwithstanding.”
biblical_def: Howbeit is the KJV’s great word of turning — “nevertheless, however, be it as it may” — the hinge on which a sentence pivots from one truth to a weightier one. It can mark the blindness of unbelief: “Howbeit we know this man whence he is: but when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is” (Joh 7:27) — the “howbeit” introducing the false certainty that shut Jerusalem’s eyes to her own Messiah. It can guard the weak conscience: “Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge” (1Co 8:7), Paul turning from the freedom of the strong to the tenderness owed the weak. It can name the one weapon for a stubborn evil: “Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting” (Mat 17:21). And it can lay bare the searching hand of God: “Howbeit in the business of the ambassadors… God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart” (2Ch 32:31) — Hezekiah’s pride exposed by the very silence of God. In each place the little word does heavy work: it refuses to let the first clause stand alone, and bends the reader toward the deeper or the truer thing. The Scripture reasons; it qualifies; it turns. Let the reader learn to feel the weight of every “howbeit,” for the whole difference between error and truth, presumption and grace, often hangs upon it.
webster_summary: “Nevertheless, however” — the KJV’s hinge-word that turns a sentence from one truth toward a weightier one.
webster_full: HOWBEIT, nevertheless; however; be it as it may; yet notwithstanding.
A compound of “how,” “be,” and “it” — “how(ever) it be.”
It introduces the false certainty of unbelief (Joh 7:27).
It turns the strong toward the weak conscience (1Co 8:7).
It names the one cure for a stubborn evil: prayer and fasting (Mat 17:21).
scriptures: Joh 7:27
Howbeit we know this man whence he is: but when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is.
Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge: for some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled.
Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.

Howbeit in the business of the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land, God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a lost conjunction; recovering it restores the sinews of Scripture’s reasoning — the turns on which truth hangs.
corruption_paragraphs: The loss the word marks is the loss of careful reading. Scripture argues; it qualifies; it turns on words like “howbeit,” “nevertheless,” “but God.” An age that reads in fragments, hunting a verse to feel and skipping the hinge that governs it, misses the very logic of revelation. Jerusalem’s fatal “howbeit we know this man” (Joh 7:27) shows how a confident clause, left unturned, can shut the eyes against Christ. The hinges are where the reasoning lives.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverent, connected reading — feeling the weight of every turn the Spirit gives His argument. “Howbeit” refuses to let a half-truth stand; it bends us toward the weaker brother, the harder cure, the searching of God. To honor the conjunctions of Scripture is to honor its Author’s reasoning, and to read as men who would be taught, not merely stirred (2Ti 2:15).
roots_summary: “How it be” — a homely English compound that became the KJV’s strong word for “nevertheless,” the hinge of its reasoning.
roots_lines: Howbeit — “how,” “be,” “it”: literally “how(ever) it be.”
It means nevertheless, however, yet notwithstanding.
It marks the false certainty that hid Christ from Jerusalem (Joh 7:27).
It turns the strong to spare the weak conscience (1Co 8:7).
It names the cure for stubborn evil: prayer and fasting (Mat 17:21).
usage: The whole difference between error and truth may hang on a howbeit.
Scripture reasons and turns; learn to feel the weight of the hinge.
Howbeit refuses to let the first clause stand alone.

etymology: From Old English sithþan (“after that, since”), the older, fuller form that contracted into the modern “since”; meaning “seeing that,” “inasmuch as,” or “because.”
biblical_def: Sith is the elder form of “since,” carrying both its senses — “from the time that” and, as here, the causal “seeing that, because.” It stands once in the KJV, in the oracle against Mount Seir: “I will prepare thee unto blood, and blood shall pursue thee: sith thou hast not hated blood, even blood shall pursue thee” (Eze 35:6). The word is the fulcrum of a fearful justice. Because Edom did not hate the shedding of blood — loved it, rather, and shed his brother Israel’s in the day of calamity (Eze 35:5) — blood is appointed to hunt him down. The sin names the sentence: the man who will not hate blood shall be pursued by it. Here is the ancient law written large: “Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed” (Gen 9:6), for man bears the image of God, and violence against the image is answered in kind. Our Lord seals the same principle: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). The little “sith” binds crime to consequence with an iron logic — not arbitrary wrath, but the moral order of a God who requires the blood of the innocent. Edom’s doom hangs on that hinge, and so does every unrepented cruelty; the God who says “sith thou hast not hated blood” still governs a world where sin summons its own pursuer.
webster_summary: The old, fuller form of “since,” meaning “seeing that” or “because” — the hinge of judgment on bloodguilty Edom.
webster_full: SITH, since; seeing that; inasmuch as; because.

It binds Edom’s crime to its sentence: blood shall pursue the lover of blood.
The causal “sith” names the sin that names the doom.
scriptures: Eze 35:6
Therefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will prepare thee unto blood, and blood shall pursue thee: sith thou hast not hated blood, even blood shall pursue thee.
Eze 35:5
Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end:
Gen 9:6
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an obsolete conjunction; it recovers the causal logic of divine justice — the sin that summons its own sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the age’s severing of deed from consequence. “Sith thou hast not hated blood” ties Edom’s doom straight to Edom’s cruelty; the sentence is not arbitrary but earned. A generation that will not hate the shedding of innocent blood — that shrugs at violence, at the destruction of the image of God in the weak and unborn — stands under the same causal “sith.” Sin is never idle; it summons its own pursuer, and blood cries from the ground (Gen 4:10).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the moral coherence of God’s judgments: He gives reasons, and the reason is our sin. “Sith” is the hinge that keeps justice from looking like caprice — the LORD says why. Against this stands the only refuge, the blood that speaketh better things than that of Abel (Heb 12:24), which pleads not vengeance but mercy for all who hate their sin and flee to Christ.
roots_summary: The elder form of “since,” “sith” means “because” — the causal hinge fastening Edom’s cruelty to Edom’s doom.

etymology: From Old English ær, “earlier, before” (the source also of “early” and “erst”); a conjunction and preposition meaning “before” in time.
biblical_def: Ere means simply “before” — before in time — but the KJV loves to hang urgent things upon it, so that the little word again and again marks the narrow margin between life and death, mercy and judgment. The Hebrew midwives report that the Hebrew women “are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them” (Exo 1:19), the child in the world before the hand of death could reach it — God’s providence outrunning Pharaoh’s murder. In the temple the boy Samuel is called “ere the lamp of God went out” (1Sa 3:3): the word of the LORD comes in the last of the night, before the light quite failed, a picture of God speaking in the dimmest hour of a slumbering church. In the wilderness judgment strikes with terrible speed — the quails “yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed” (Num 11:33) — lust cut off in the very moment of its indulgence. And the nobleman cries, “Sir, come down ere my child die” (Joh 4:49), faith racing against the clock, only to learn that Christ’s word needs no such haste. Ere marks the margin of time in which everything is decided — the “before” that will not wait. It is the word of urgency: seek the LORD ere He hide His face, repent ere the door is shut, for the day of grace has an “ere,” and no man knows how near it stands.
webster_summary: “Before” in time — the KJV’s word of urgency, marking the narrow margin in which everything is decided.
webster_full: ERE, before; sooner than; previous to a time or event.
From Old English ær, “earlier”; kin to “early” and “erst.”
Samuel is called “ere the lamp of God went out” (1Sa 3:3).
Judgment falls ere the quail is chewed (Num 11:33).
“Come down ere my child die” — faith against the clock (Joh 4:49).
scriptures: Exo 1:19
And the midwives said unto Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them.
And ere the lamp of God went out in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was, and Samuel was laid down to sleep;
And while the flesh was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD smote the people with a very great plague.
Joh 4:49
The nobleman saith unto him, Sir, come down ere my child die.
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under dispute but a fading word for “before”; recovering it recovers the Bible’s note of urgency — the margin of time that will not wait.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the presumption that there is always time. Ere is the margin, and the margin closes. The quail was still between their teeth, ere it was chewed, when wrath fell (Num 11:33); the door of the ark shut ere the flood; the foolish virgins came to buy oil, and while they went, the bridegroom came. An age that means to repent later, believe later, obey later, has forgotten the “ere.” Today, while it is called today, is the whole of what we are given (Heb 3:15).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is holy urgency — to seek the LORD while He may be found, ere He hide His face; to make peace with the adversary ere the officer deliver us to the judge (Mat 5:25). The lamp of God had not yet gone out when Samuel was called; God still speaks in the dim last hour, but there is an “ere” beyond which grace does not reach. Boast not thyself of to morrow (Pro 27:1).
roots_summary: From Old English ær, “before,” “ere” marks the KJV’s narrow margin of time in which mercy and judgment are decided.

etymology: From Old English on ān, “into one, in one (moment)” — that is, at once; an adverb meaning “straightway, immediately, presently.”
biblical_def: Anon means “straightway, at once, immediately,” born of the Old English phrase “in one moment.” It stands twice in the KJV, and in both places it marks a swift response — but the two could not be more different in what they teach. In the parable of the sower, the stony-ground hearer “heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it” (Mat 13:20); the very speed is the flaw. His quick, glad reception has no root, and “dureth for a while,” so that “when tribulation or persecution ariseth… by and by he is offended” (Mat 13:21). Anon received, anon offended: shallow soil warms fast and dries fast, and the emotion that leaps up in a moment withers in a moment. Against this stands the “anon” of true and needful haste: “Simon’s wife’s mother lay sick of a fever, and anon they tell him of her” (Mar 1:30), and the Lord straightway heals her, and she straightway ministers (Mar 1:31). Here quickness is faith — bringing the need at once to Christ, and rising at once to serve. So the word sets two speeds side by side: the hasty joy that has no root, and the ready faith that runs to Jesus with its trouble. The question is never merely whether a man responds anon, but what abides when the first quickness is spent — whether there was root beneath the leaf.
webster_summary: “Straightway, immediately” — contrasting the rootless haste of the stony hearer with the ready faith that runs to Christ.
webster_full: ANON, straightway; immediately; at once; presently.
From Old English on ān, “in one (moment).”
The stony hearer “anon with joy receiveth” the word (Mat 13:20).
That quickness has no root and withers in trouble (Mat 13:21).
“Anon they tell him” of the fever — haste of faith (Mar 1:30).
scriptures: But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;
Mar 1:30
But Simon's wife's mother lay sick of a fever, and anon they tell him of her.
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
Mar 1:31
And he came and took her by the hand, and lifted her up; and immediately the fever left her, and she ministered unto them.
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under dispute but a lost word for “at once”; it recovers the warning that quick joy without root is no saving faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the shallow religion of the sudden. The stony hearer receives anon, with joy, and the age applauds exactly such quick warm responses — the instant decision, the emotional high, the fast profession. But anon received is anon offended; soil that warms fast dries fast, and the man who had no root endures only for a while. Christ Himself teaches us to distrust a joy that has not been tested by tribulation. What comes up in a night can wither in a day.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is rootedness — that the worth of a response is proved not by its speed but by what abides when trouble comes. There is a good “anon,” the haste of faith that runs at once to Christ with its trouble and rises at once to serve Him (Mar 1:30-31); and there is a deadly one, the quick joy without depth of earth. Let the reader see that he be rooted and grounded (Eph 3:17), lest he be a hearer only, and anon offended.
roots_summary: From Old English on ān, “in one moment,” “anon” means “straightway” — the speed that saves or the speed that shames.

usage: Anon received, anon offended: quick joy withered in the heat.
